text: Release cadence and upgrade timelines both assume the platform is in reasonably good shape underneath. It often isn't. This lesson is about technical debt, the accumulated shortcuts that make every future change harder and riskier than it should be.

Technical debt is not just old code, or a feature nobody uses. It's a shortcut taken for an understandable reason at the time, that makes future changes harder and riskier than they should be. Like financial debt, it was taken on to move faster now, and it accrues interest: every later change to that area of the platform costs more time and more risk than it would have otherwise.

Three sources show up constantly on real instances. Deadline shortcuts, like a Business Rule that hard-codes a sys_id instead of a proper reference because the real fix needed more time than the go-live date allowed. Deprecated API reliance, which Lesson 21 flagged as an upgrade risk, but is really a standing debt that widens every release cycle it survives. And undocumented customizations, where the original developer is long gone and nobody currently on the team fully understands what a Script Include does or why, so nobody wants to touch it even when it's causing real problems.

The architect's responsibility is finding this debt before it causes an incident, not after. Waiting for the hard-coded value to break in production, or for the deprecated API to actually get removed mid-upgrade, means the fix happens under the worst possible conditions: unplanned, urgent, no room to do it properly. That means actively auditing deprecated-API flags, reviewing scripts for hard-coded values, and keeping a running, visible list, rather than letting the knowledge live only in individual developers' heads.

Finding the debt is the easy part. The recurring, harder part is prioritizing remediation against constant pressure to ship new features, when the business stakeholder asking for the next capability doesn't see the risk you're trying to defuse. A real case for remediation names what the debt is costing today, what deferring it past a known event like an upgrade will cost, and, often most persuasively, what it's currently blocking.

That third argument reframes debt remediation as removing an obstacle to something the organization already wants, rather than a competing priority against it. Next up: the lifecycle management lab, a worked scenario that pulls upgrade planning, release cadence, and technical debt together into one real decision.
